intro.lead: Welcome to **Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu**, widely recognized as the central **People's Freedom Arch** of Kyiv. Located in the heart of **Kyiv**, **Ukraine**, high above the Dnipro River, this free riverside landmark serves as a primary hub for travelers exploring the capital and a gateway to Mariinskyi Palace, the Kyiv Funicular and the historic Pechersk district.
intro.title: About Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu
intro.description: Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu is located in Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine. It is an important historical monument and tourist attraction. This magnificent arch witnessed the historical process of the Ukrainian people's pursuit of freedom and independence, and is an important place to feel the Ukrainian national spirit. It was unveiled in 1982 as the People's Friendship Arch and officially renamed the Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People in 2022.

history.title: History & Significance of Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu
paragraphs: The sweeping rainbow-shaped arch was opened on 7 November 1982, when Kyiv celebrated its 1,500th anniversary. It was erected to mark the 60th anniversary of the USSR and the 1654 Pereiaslav agreement, and was originally known as the People's Friendship Arch (Ukrainian: Арка дружби народів). The composition was designed by sculptor Oleksandr Skoblikov together with architects Serhiy Myrhorodsky, Kostiantyn Sydorov and I. Ivanov.

For four decades the monument symbolized the idea of friendship between the Ukrainian and Russian peoples: beneath the arch stood a bronze sculpture group and a granite stele decorated with the Order of Friendship of Peoples. In April 2022 the Soviet-era bronze composition was dismantled, and the Kyiv authorities renamed the monument Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu - the Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People.

Today the towering metal arc, rising about 35 metres (115 ft) above the Dnipro riverfront in Khreshchatyi Park, is widely read as a symbol of Ukrainian freedom and independence. It remains free to visit around the clock and is one of the most photographed landmarks in Kyiv.
facts: Opened on 7 November 1982 during the 1,500th anniversary celebrations of Kyiv
Location: Khreshchatyi Park, Parkova Doroha, Kyiv
Renamed in April 2022 to Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu
history.quote1: It was not built as a monument to a friendship between equals: it opened in 1982 within the commemorative context of the USSR’s 60th anniversary, promoting the official “friendship of Soviet peoples” narrative of that era.
history.quote2: The 2022 renaming did not erase history — it renamed it. The arch turned from celebrating the old union toward marking the freedom of the Ukrainian people.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.note: Quick answers about the location, access and history of People's Freedom Arch.

items.q: Where is Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu located?
items.a: Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu stands in Khreshchatyi Park on Parkova Doroha, Kyiv, Ukraine, 02000 (Plus Code FG3H+QX), on the high right bank of the Dnipro River with a riverside viewing deck.

items.q: Is the Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People free to visit?
items.a: Yes. The monument is a public open-air landmark inside a city park, and access is completely free, 24 hours a day, all year round - no ticket or reservation is required.

items.q: Why was the arch originally built?
items.a: The arch was opened on 7 November 1982 during Kyiv's 1,500th anniversary celebrations to mark the 60th anniversary of the USSR and the 1654 Pereiaslav agreement. It was originally named the People's Friendship Arch and was designed by sculptor Oleksandr Skoblikov with architects Serhiy Myrhorodsky, Kostiantyn Sydorov and I. Ivanov.

items.q: Why is it now called the Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People?
items.a: In April 2022 the monument was renamed Arka Svobody Ukrayinsʹkoho Narodu (Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People). The Soviet-era bronze sculpture group beneath the arch was dismantled, and today the arch is widely seen as a symbol of Ukrainian freedom and independence.
The sweeping metal arc rises about 35 metres (115 ft) high and forms a recognizable rainbow-shaped curve above the Dnipro riverfront, making it a favourite photo spot at any time of day.

items.q: When is the best time to visit the arch?
items.a: Sunrise and late afternoon offer the softest light, and spring and autumn bring the most comfortable temperatures. In summer, visit in the morning or in the evening, when the monument is also illuminated at night.

items.q: How do I get to the People's Freedom Arch?
items.a: The closest metro station is Arsenalna (about a 15-20 minute walk through Mariinskyi Park). Buses and trolleybuses stop along Parkova Doroha, while the Kyiv Funicular and taxi services also reach the area.

items.q: What else can I combine with a visit to the arch?
items.a: The arch sits between Mariinskyi Park and Khreshchatyi Park, close to Mariinskyi Palace, the Kyiv Funicular and European Square. Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, Maidan Nezalezhnosti and the Dnipro embankment are also easy to include in one walk.

services.title: Visitor Services & Nearby Facilities
services.subtitle: This nonprofit science website lists facility types only as a neutral overview. We do not recommend or rank any specific business or brand — please confirm details on site.

items.name: Public toilets
items.desc: The arch plaza is open public space and usually has no fixed toilets; the nearest are typically inside adjacent metro stations, shopping centres, park entrances and dining streets.

items.name: Water & supplies
items.desc: Benches line the park paths and riverside walk, but public drinking fountains are scarce — bring your own water; bottled water is widely sold at convenience stores.

items.name: Rest & shade
items.desc: Shaded benches and groves along the park and riverside allow frequent breaks; in strong midday sun, prefer walking under the trees.

items.name: Dining (by type)
items.desc: The landmark and the hillside commercial streets offer local cuisine, casual eateries, coffee bakeries, desserts and fast food of every price range; peaks around 1–3 pm.

items.name: Lodging (by type)
items.desc: Hotels, apartments, hostels and guesthouses are available across the city centre; choosing one near a metro line makes early and late exploring easier.

items.name: Supermarkets & shops
items.desc: Convenience stores are widespread downtown for water, snacks and basic pharmacy items; larger supermarkets and malls cover bulk shopping a bit further out.

items.name: Parking
items.desc: On-street parking near the landmark is limited and mostly paid by time; it fills up on weekends and holidays. Public transport is recommended, or park at an outlying lot and transfer.

items.name: EV charging
items.desc: Charging stations are progressively available at major hotels, commercial areas and some car parks; check live availability on charging platforms.

items.name: Fuel stations
items.desc: Branded and independent stations inside the city and on ring roads provide petrol and diesel; plan ahead before long self-drive trips.

items.name: Public transport links
items.desc: Metro, buses, trolleybuses and bike share connect the area; transport cards can be obtained at main metro stations.

items.name: Payment & currency
items.desc: The local currency is the hryvnia (₴). Bank cards and mobile payments are widely accepted downtown; keep a little cash for small or urgent purchases.

items.name: Information services
items.desc: City visitor points and bookshops provide maps, guides and transit brochures; tourism information is authoritative when issued by city authorities and official platforms.

tips: The landmark is a free, open public space with no on-site facilities — plan your own food and supply stops;
Rush hours (roughly 8–9 am and 5–7 pm) make metro and buses crowded — schedule visits off-peak;
With large luggage, pushchairs or mobility aids, choose metro stations with lifts and step-free entrances;
Keep valuables close and watch your bags and phone outdoors.

seasons.title: Seasonal Visit Strategy
seasons.lead: Turn “when to go” into a science question: the table below combines seasonal climate, riverside hydrology and urban wildlife patterns with visit and photography advice.
seasons.basis: Based on Kyiv long-term observational averages for the 1991–2020 climate normal period. Use it for yearly planning — always check the live weather on this page for your travel day.

rows.weather: Warming but still cool: about 1–8 °C in March, rising to 14–20 °C by May; rain increases and days warm up quickly.
rows.water: The Dnipro is in spring flood — higher and faster water, wide views but strong river wind; mind slippery steps and rails.
rows.nature: Migratory birds pass through, trees bud and blossom — a prime time for birding and plant photography.
rows.visit: Soft light in morning and evening with fewer visitors; carry a windproof jacket and a foldable umbrella.

rows.weather: Typically 22–30 °C by day with occasional heat spikes; afternoon thundershowers are possible, nights are cooler.
rows.water: River cruises and waterside activity peak and the embankment gets busy; follow official notices about water and safety — swimming is not advised.
rows.nature: Dense shade and active mornings; birds sing at dawn, and urban wildlife is most visible early and late.
rows.visit: Best in the early morning or after sunset; protect against the sun at noon and expect weekend crowds.

rows.weather: Comfortable September (about 14–20 °C), cooling in October and early winter by November (about 0–5 °C); morning fog and rain increase.
rows.water: Autumn flood is gentle; morning mist over the river makes atmospheric photos, and the low sun returns by November.
rows.nature: Golden foliage and active squirrels — one of the best seasons to observe urban ecology.
rows.visit: October delivers some of the year’s best photos: low-angle light and saturated colours at dawn and dusk.

rows.weather: Averages about -6–0 °C with snowfall and slippery roads; occasional cold snaps demand warm layers.
rows.water: The river usually does not freeze over; thin ice may appear in shallow inlets only in extreme cold — never walk on ice.
rows.nature: Quiet snowy parks reveal resident birds and footprints in the snow; short days call for extra lighting care.
rows.visit: Festive lights make December evenings beautiful; wear warm, slip-resistant footwear and mind battery drain in the cold.

seasons.note: Note: temperatures are historical averages, not day-specific forecasts; river conditions and wildlife observation spots vary year to year.

routes.title: Recommended General Routes
routes.lead: Independent of any tour product, the half-day or full-day rhythm below lets an ordinary visitor enjoy the landmark and its classic backdrop at ease. Both routes are free and can be shortened at any point.

items.label: Half-day essentials
items.time: About 3–4 hours · mostly walking and viewpoints
points: Enter from the riverside gate and take in the Dnipro and the opposite skyline from the deck (about 20 min)
Walk the plaza axis to the arch; study the rainbow curve and the ground inscriptions (about 30 min)
Stroll the Mariinskyi Park avenues, resting and refilling water on benches (about 40 min)
Descend toward European Square and leave by metro, bus or bike share (about 30 min)
items.note: Ideal for arrival day or a tight schedule — the shortest walk that still covers the core views and classic backdrop.

items.label: Full-day in depth
items.time: About 6–8 hours · with breaks and meals
points: Morning: arch — viewing deck — Mariinskyi Park for early light; the Mariinskyi Palace is ceremonial and can be viewed from outside only
Noon: eat as you wish in the commercial quarter, away from the hottest sun and rush lines
Afternoon: follow the slope into the old upper town, linking historic cathedral sites and old lanes
Evening: return to the riverside for sunset and the city lights panorama
items.note: Best for visitors staying a day or more who want to combine the landmark with the old town; evening light on the river is a highlight.

routes.common: General: no booking needed; wear comfortable shoes, bring rain gear or warm layers by season, keep valuables close and travel responsibly.

responsibility.title: Science & Visitor Responsibility
responsibility.lead: This is a public space that remembers a city’s shared history. It deserves to be understood — and protected by every visitor.

blocks.title: Learn before you go
blocks.text: Check official safety notices and weather, confirm metro operation and your documents; follow on-site signs and restricted areas on arrival.

blocks.title: Record with your eyes, don’t touch history
blocks.text: Never climb the arch or pedestals, carve, scribble or pull at installations — keep this memorial space dignified and intact for the future.

blocks.title: Leave no trace
blocks.text: Put rubbish in the bins or carry it out; clean up after picnics and dispose of cigarette butts and glass responsibly.

blocks.title: Respect the life around you
blocks.text: Do not feed or chase birds, squirrels or other animals; when observing or photographing, stay calm, quiet and at a respectful distance.

blocks.title: Share the space with others
blocks.text: Yield to others and keep noise low in busy hours; consider off-peak visits so everyone gets the best view.

blocks.title: Use photography equipment lawfully
blocks.text: Tripods and drones are subject to local rules and on-site signs; do not photograph private interiors or sensitive facilities without permission.

items.text: Resolution No. 597 of the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR (28 Dec 1979) approved a “Friendship of Peoples” memorial complex in Kyiv.

items.title: Unveiled
items.text: The arch was unveiled on 7 November 1982, timed with Kyiv’s 1500th anniversary and the USSR’s 60th. The arch itself is a silver arc of titanium alloy, about 35 m high and 50 m wide, with a 6.2 m bronze pair sculpture and a granite composition commemorating the 1654 Pereiaslav Council beneath it.

items.title: Temporary “Arch of Diversity”
items.text: During the Eurovision Song Contest 2017 the arch was temporarily painted in rainbow colours and presented as the “Arch of Diversity”.

items.title: Bronze sculpture removed
items.text: After the mayor’s announcement, the bronze “friendship of peoples” group beneath the arch was dismantled on 26 April 2022; the arch itself stayed.

items.title: Officially renamed
items.text: The Kyiv City Council voted to rename the monument the “Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People” (Арка Свободи українського народу).

items.title: Granite composition removed and stored
items.text: The red-granite composition on the Pereiaslav theme was dismantled and handed to the State Aviation Museum for storage; the arch remains and now carries a new meaning — freedom of the Ukrainian people.

myths.title: Myth-busting: common misconceptions
myths.lead: Many claims circulate about this arch. We check each one against resolutions, archives and reputable media.

items.claim: The arch is just painted steel or stainless steel; the “titanium” story is marketing.
items.fact: Not so: the arch is indeed clad in titanium alloy (built 1978–1982). Titanium gives it the signature silvery gloss that needs no regular repainting.

items.claim: The arch represents “Russian–Ukrainian friendship” and was built jointly by the two states.
items.fact: It was initiated by the Soviet-era Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR (Resolution No. 597, 1979) for Soviet anniversaries and promoted the official “friendship of peoples” idea. It also included a granite composition on the 1654 Pereiaslav Council, making the theme more complex than “friendship”. It was not a project of two sovereign states.

items.claim: In April 2022 the whole arch was demolished.
items.fact: On 26 April 2022 only the bronze pair sculpture under the arch was dismantled; the arch itself was not demolished. On 14 May 2022 the Kyiv City Council renamed it the “Arch of Freedom of the Ukrainian People”. On 30 April 2024 the granite composition was also removed and preserved.

items.claim: After the renaming, the old “Arch of Friendship” vanished from history.
items.fact: The old name and the bronze group were abolished, but history was not erased: the metal arch still stands, and the old name and events remain documented in archives and scholarship. That is why this site always cites both the new and the former name.
